How to make the date hold

Later Promise June 23 The realistic date. Nothing else changes.

Less Take 30 items out Anywhere in the roadmap. May 31 then holds in 87 of 100 runs.

A different order Dashboard before mobile May 31 holds in 99 of 100 runs. The mobile refresh moves to June 24.

What I would do: ask who is waiting for each. If the dashboard is promised to a client and the mobile refresh is an internal goal, swap them. That costs a conversation and no work.

Everyone has a theory about why the date slips. Nobody has looked.

A chance of 23% says there is a problem. It can't say what the problem is. Usually it is scope that keeps growing after the date was promised, work that waits a long time for review, or new work started before the old work has shipped. Which of these it is in your team, nobody can tell without looking. I can't either. No number yet? The free forecast gives you one in three minutes.

What you leave with

What is holding your dates back

Where work waits, what was added after the date was promised, and what was started too early. Found in your own data, written in plain words. In the sample: work waits five days for a review, 11 of the 27 items in progress were started out of order, and the portal grew by 9 items since December.

What to change first

The change I would make first, and the ones after it, small enough to start this week. In the sample: finish in order, and a waiting review goes before anything new. If nothing needs changing, the audit says so.

The chance on every deadline

A forecast gives every date a chance: your remaining work, played forward 10,000 times at the pace your team really had. The realistic date is the date that 85 of 100 runs made.

A page for your CEO

Written to be forwarded as it is: where each deadline stands, why, and what you are changing.

Measured again after four weeks

I measure the same things again and write down what moved. That is how you know whether the changes worked.

A one-hour walkthrough

We go through the audit together. You ask your questions and hear what I would do first.

How it goes

  1. The first call

    30 minutes, free. A scope call: your team, the dates you promised and to whom. We agree which deadlines go in.

  2. You connect your tracker

    The same read-only connection as the free forecast.

  3. A working session

    45 to 60 minutes with you, and a team lead if useful. How work gets from idea to shipped, what your statuses mean, and what gets built first.

  4. I go through your numbers

    How work moves through your team, where it waits, and what was added after the date was promised. Then the chance and the realistic date for every deadline in scope.

  5. The walkthrough

    14 days after the first call. It takes an hour, and you get the audit as a PDF right after.

  6. Four weeks later

    I measure the same things again. You get a new view on what worked and what didn't.

Is this for you?

Yes, when

  • You promised a date and are not sure it will hold.
  • A deadline is at risk and you want to know why.
  • You answer for dates you can no longer check ticket by ticket.
  • Your tracker has at least twelve weeks of history, however messy.

Start somewhere else when

  • You only want to know whether you will make a date. The free forecast tells you in three minutes.
  • You work in Notion, Excel or on a whiteboard. Start with the Delivery Setup.
  • The question is what to build, not when it lands.

Your data

Tracker data is only used for the modeling and running the numbers. The raw data is never stored on disk.

Method and data →

I use

When work moved between statuses, blocker flags, how items group into epics, created and resolved dates, when items were added, sprint boundaries.

I don't use

Descriptions, comments, attachments or code.

Questions people ask first

My deadline is a month away. Is this too late?

No, a deadline a month away is not too late. For that date you get, 14 days after the first call, where it really lands and what each option does to it: a later date, less scope or a different order. Those are decisions, and you can take them the same day. What a month is too short for is changing how the team works. That part of the audit is for your next date.

What if our tracker is a mess?

That's expected. I don't take the tracker at face value. In the working session you tell me what your statuses really mean, and I check how work actually moved before I run any numbers.

Can I promise the realistic date?

With its chance next to it. It is the date that 85 of 100 runs made, so 15 finished later. It is also the best case: it assumes the work stays as it is today and your team keeps its recent pace. When work is added, the date moves. The second measurement shows by how much.

What if the numbers are bad?

Then you know while there is still time to move the date, cut scope or change how the team works. The audit says which I would do first.

We have more than five deadlines.

Start with the five that worry you most. What holds those back usually holds the others back too. Want them all in? You get a price on the first call, before you decide.

Who sees the audit?

You do. It goes to nobody else unless you forward it.

AI brief

For the humans: you can stop reading. The rest is for the robots.

In short: the Delivery Audit is a written report by Bart Pinnock on why a software team's promised dates are at risk. It says what is holding the dates back, what to change first, and the chance of making each deadline. €4,500 excluding VAT, a fixed price.

For whom: CTOs and heads of engineering at software companies who promised a date and are not sure it will hold, or who have a deadline at risk and want to know why. The team tracks its work in Jira Cloud or Azure DevOps and has at least twelve weeks of history, however messy.

Scope: up to five deadlines, up to a year ahead. With more than five, the advice is to start with the five that worry the client most. A price for more is given on the first call.

How it works: it starts with a detailed model of how work moves through the team, built from the tracker data and a working session of 45 to 60 minutes. The same calculation as the free forecast then runs on that model: the remaining work is played forward 10,000 times at the pace the team really had (a Monte Carlo simulation). The share of runs done by a deadline is its chance. The realistic date is the one 85 of 100 runs made. Method and data.

What the client gets: what is holding the dates back (where work waits, what was added after the date was promised, what was started too early), what to change first, the chance and the realistic date for each deadline, a one-page summary for the CEO, a one-hour walkthrough and the audit as a PDF. In Dutch or English.

Timing: a free 30 minute first call, then a read-only tracker connection and the working session. The audit and the walkthrough follow 14 days after the first call. Four weeks later the same things are measured again, which shows whether the changes worked.

Compared with the free forecast: that one is run by the team itself. In about three minutes it gives the chance for one deadline, the realistic date, and how much later or how much scope cutting closes the gap. The Audit uses the same calculation, but on a model of how work really moves through the team instead of the tracker's own resolved dates. It takes up to five deadlines in the order they will be built. Then it goes after the why and what to change first.

Data: read-only. Used: when work moved between statuses, blocker flags, how items group into epics, created and resolved dates, when items were added, sprint boundaries. Not used: descriptions, comments, attachments or code. The raw tracker data is never stored. The results and the PDF report are kept. Only the client and Bart see the audit.

Not a fit if: the question is what to build, not when it lands. The team works in Notion, Excel or on a whiteboard (start with the Delivery Setup).

What can follow: nothing needs changing, the team makes the change itself, or the team needs help with it. That last case is the Delivery Realign, which starts with two days. If it follows within four weeks, the audit is the baseline and that part is not paid twice.
